document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

4E5909F472B44E3DAA903818636F46AC.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

E2DB2EBB9541444E9069F60F89E24C97.description: Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.
comments: Example: express 3 in the form 3 = 3/1; recognize that 6/1 = 6.
Example: locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point of a number line diagram.

EBBF5C3565424631A2612A280CBDD986.description: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3). Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

D8DF7833E0E44B738FB9EC61D5B640E4.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line.

217B4DFB03864F81BD90453A735BBBDB.description: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.

390E191CEAD3446DB281E961296B0F7F.description: Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line.

8489DF463D7A416FB3B3C59819C1CB48.description: Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line.

7D8519468F364BCE8CBE52BBB84DDF71.description: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.

3CC43E83A34345B488252382B7CD4728.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b.

50049B05EF264C4AA61A2A5EBAD24B44.description: Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100
For example, partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area, and describe the area of each part as 1/4 of the area of the shape.
E31F4EB8D2E24D059CFC580EC6F10CD3.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.

5E80110A63144E38BDBEA912F6E86C2A.description: Understand that shapes in different categories (e.g., rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (e.g., having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category (e.g., quadrilaterals). Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.

5E292E90EFF74ACAB2D2C9E7FF143A72.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

95F2812DBBF449A8B999880497923AC8.description: Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.

C8833762B72D46B69A82389DC5BE899D.description: Geometric measurement: recognize perimeter as an attribute of plane figures and distinguish between linear and area measures.

EB63A753DD12437EB5987FEEDAB8FC23.description: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.

7B9A0383E5A74B44A1006A3DD49FC362.description: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.

871BFB43F8E54DC79C3E5CD5A04A14B2.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.

F340BF1FD31C4185BDEB7EC286DF1B84.description: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.

E9A85878F7C9477683E44238DB366AAC.description: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition.

EC386AC95A4649EDBF8285CEB80FCFE0.description: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft, and improvised units).

AE777708CAC9461393398188BDABF0AC.description: A plane figure which can be covered without gaps or overlaps by n unit squares is said to have an area of n square units.

7B44F8A2EF1142C69860EEF18739DB1B.description: A square with side length 1 unit, called "a unit square," is said to have "one square unit" of area, and can be used to measure area.

FB0374681AC6447081D931AA4362B4C1.description: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement.

A245984E3D4C4B54803093F72FB92505.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of area and relate area to multiplication and to addition.

93B625295B294C4A96CDAC0109E70653.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units— whole numbers, halves, or quarters.

CAF6D0E8E3CB4D928B0C528E13020804.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step "how many more" and "how many less" problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.
comments: For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.

768FB7765BCD4D31B1B22A909501C73D.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), and liters (l). Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or volumes that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as a beaker with a measurement scale) to represent the problem.
comments: Excludes multiplicative comparison problems (problems involving notions of "times as much";
Excludes compound units such as cm³ and finding the geometric volume of a container.

4D31EEB750954D86ACF8AF5E47405115.description: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in minutes. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes, e.g., by representing the problem on a number line diagram.

544D1D004ADD4AEAA7FE17F8EA98B017.description: Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid volumes, and masses of objects.

21DC2E5836F94675BB054951C9FDB207.description: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10—90 (e.g., 9 × 80, 5 × 60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

DEA1FE18547B4412AC09CB87E3CB8D07.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

844BD03E9389488BAEB7E28DAD9B58DA.description: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.

A6BFBE762F79434FAB8838B80D19B279.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
comments: A range of algorithms may be used.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.
6305DE912B5E48A0BE7F671BCEE76297.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

comments: For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.
F9C81207B7F44503918DDE724C2C1B17.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations.

comments: This standard is limited to problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers; students should know how to perform operations in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).
F787449D70B64119BA5245B341D1B957.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.

CC46EA9BAAA340B8BC75FB6BF810FD9A.description: Solve problems involving the four operations, and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.

6780A9EB67BB430181976766CDF0BDAE.description: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.

D0626362BF634643B0CECEC1B0F7FE03.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem.
comments: For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.

B3028EC4A8634E65980BDE5870644FBB.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
Example: Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.)

Example: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.)

4DB26670A66146C4902B78153357E9CB.description: Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.

59522F9225D84B29AAD0F3727E7054F4.description: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 × ? = 48, 5 = ÷ 3, 6 × 6 = ?.

56B0DD78CD8548F8BD9DE707160AD814.description: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D6B583CCCEA3415C9499F32914C493E0.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8.

B3C6EC95DE01427DBA9F9BF02FFB0254.description: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a total number of objects can be expressed as 5 × 7.

1A73B353185347CDAEF311860AB4275D.description: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
A05DC87CDA3D4592AB28CB95E05AE0DD.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

75805564459846C7AC2A8DCDF30A613D.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

9F64B89A1DA146169127340B07C2DB5B.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

FC499C62070442368303AEC14904EFD9.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Delaware Theatre Content Standards and Grade Level Expectations

DF111D10DFE40131359568A86D17958E.description: Assess how an audience's response can impact a theatrical presentation

DF10BCA0DFE40131359468A86D17958E.description: Relate the elements of a dramatic production and the impact they have on the viewer

DF106BA0DFE40131359368A86D17958E.description: Identify and employ techniques for active listening and viewing of theatrical productions

DF103150DFE40131359268A86D17958E.description: Responding to, describing, analyzing, interpreting, and evaluating theatre works and performances

DF0FF6B0DFE40131359168A86D17958E.description: Incorporate elements of dance, music, and visual arts to express ideas and emotions in improvised and structured scenes

DF0FBC00DFE40131359068A86D17958E.description: Observe different forms of communication and transfer them into usage in performance (verbal, nonverbal, ASL, written, iconic, etc.)

DF0F80A0DFE40131358F68A86D17958E.description: Observe examples of role playing in life and analyze how those roles could be used by theatre artists

DF0E72A0DFE40131358B68A86D17958E.description: Develop and implement costume and makeup designs for a structured theatrical production

DF0E2F90DFE40131358A68A86D17958E.description: Designing and building environments for informal and formal presentations

DF0DE320DFE40131358968A86D17958E.description: Portray a believable character with effective performance techniques (use of voice, facial expressions and body movement) in both improvised and structured presentations

DF0D9F80DFE40131358868A86D17958E.description: Identify character motivations through research and analysis and be able to articulate how they affect the character's actions

DF0D42E0DFE40131358768A86D17958E.description: Recall and recite assigned lines for a theater piece

DF0CE860DFE40131358668A86D17958E.description: Employ variations in movement, gesture and vocal expression (pitch, tempo, tone) to create characters

DF0CA140DFE40131358568A86D17958E.description: Acting in improvised and structured presentations

DF0C5870DFE40131358468A86D17958E.description: Develop an improvisation utilizing characters and setting that creates tension and suspense, with a subsequent resolution

DF0C0CE0DFE40131358368A86D17958E.description: Identify the basic elements of a play (e.g., characters, setting, plot)

DF0BBFE0DFE40131358268A86D17958E.description: Identify the foundation of playmaking in real life and fantasy

DF0B65F0DFE40131358168A86D17958E.description: Improvising and writing scenes, scenarios and plays

F2E8CF60DFE401315AED68A86D17958E.description: Students will apply knowledge of the types of regions and methods of drawing boundaries to interpret the Earth's changing complexity.

F2E892A0DFE401315AEC68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop an understanding of the character and use of regions and the connections between and among them [REGIONS].

F2E85160DFE401315AEB68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the processes which result in distinctive cultures, economic activity, and settlement form in particular locations across the world.

F2E80A10DFE401315AEA68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop an understanding of the diversity of human culture and the unique nature of places [PLACES].

F2E7C6F0DFE401315AE968A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the Earth's physical environment as a set of interconnected systems (ecosystems) and the ways humans have perceived, reacted to, and changed environments at local to global scales.

F2E77B00DFE401315AE868A86D17958E.description: Students will develop a knowledge of the ways humans modify and respond to the natural environment [ENVIRONMENT].

F2E731B0DFE401315AE768A86D17958E.description: Students will apply the analysis of mapped patterns to the solution of problems.

F2E6E9F0DFE401315AE668A86D17958E.description:
Students will identify geographic patterns which emerge when collected data is mapped, and analyze mapped patterns through the application of such common geographic principles as
  • Hierarchy (patterns at a detailed scale may be related to patterns at a more general scale)
  • Accessibility (how easily one place can be reached from another)
  • Diffusion (how people or things move in certain directions at certain speeds)
  • Complimentarity (the mutual exchange of people or goods among places usually occurs over the shortest possible distances)

F2E69A90DFE401315AE568A86D17958E.description: Students will develop a personal geographic framework, or "mental map," and understand the uses of maps and other geo-graphics [MAPS].

DEF1D390DFE40131356C68A86D17958E.description: Describe and/or demonstrate how skills transfer between the visual arts and other disciplines

DEF14040DFE40131356A68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast relationships and characteristics between the visual arts and other disciplines

DEEF6530DFE40131356468A86D17958E.description: Describe personal responses to selected works of art

DEEF24C0DFE40131356368A86D17958E.description: Identify ways the visual arts are used as communication

DEEEE600DFE40131356268A86D17958E.description: Discuss how individual experiences influence personal works of art

DEEEA740DFE40131356168A86D17958E.description: Reflecting upon and assessing the characteristics and merits of their work and the work of others

DEEE6930DFE40131356068A86D17958E.description: Describe how the visual arts influence history and cultures

DEEE27B0DFE40131355F68A86D17958E.description: Describe how history and cultures influence the visual arts

DEEDDAE0DFE40131355E68A86D17958E.description: Describe and differentiate the roles of artists in society across history and cultures

DEED9DF0DFE40131355D68A86D17958E.description: Speculate on how history and culture give meaning to a work of art

DEED6030DFE40131355C68A86D17958E.description: Compare the purpose of works of art and design in history and cultures

DEED2160DFE40131355B68A86D17958E.description: Describe how the arts and artists influence each other across history and cultures

DEECE3B0DFE40131355A68A86D17958E.description: Identify historical and cultural characteristics of works of art

DEEC9FA0DFE40131355968A86D17958E.description: Understanding the visual arts in relation to history and cultures

DEEC5390DFE40131355868A86D17958E.description: Analyze how the use of subject matter, symbols and ideas are used in works of art

DEEC0030DFE40131355768A86D17958E.description: Describe and differentiate the origins of specific subject matter, symbols and ideas in works of art

DEEBB4E0DFE40131355668A86D17958E.description: Select and use subject matter, symbols and ideas to communicate meaning in works of art

DEEB6940DFE40131355568A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the sources for content to validate the manner in which subject matter, symbols and ideas are used in works of art

DEEADD50DFE40131355368A86D17958E.description: Identify subject matter, symbols and ideas in works of art

DEEA9600DFE40131355268A86D17958E.description: Choosing and evaluating a range of subject matter, symbols and ideas

DEE80A30DFE40131354968A86D17958E.description: Analyze how the elements of art and principles of design applied through various media, techniques and processes produce different effects

DEEA4920DFE40131355168A86D17958E.description: Plan, design and execute multiple solutions to challenging visual arts problems

DEE9FFF0DFE40131355068A86D17958E.description: Select and apply the knowledge of the elements of art and principles of design to convey ideas in works of art

DEE92FE0DFE40131354D68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate works of art in terms of structure and function

DEE72800DFE40131354668A86D17958E.description: Describe how media and techniques are used to create two-dimensional and three dimensional works of art

F1AFD880DFE40131591468A86D17958E.description: Many natural resources are limited. The amount available can be made to last longer by decreasing the use of some resources or by reusing or recycling certain materials.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Humans can alter the living and non-living factors within an ecosystem, thereby creating changes to the overall system.

F1AF3140DFE40131591268A86D17958E.description: All animals depend on plants. Some animals eat plants for food. Other animals eat animals that have eaten plants.

F1AEE2E0DFE40131591168A86D17958E.description: Energy Flow and Material Cycles in the Environment
comments: Enduring Understandings: Matter needed to sustain life is continually recycled among and between organisms and the environment. Energy from the Sun flows irreversibly through ecosystems and is conserved as organisms use and transform it.

F1AE91E0DFE40131591068A86D17958E.description: Plants and animals need enough space and resources to survive. Overcrowding leads to an increased need for resources.

F1AE49B0DFE40131590F68A86D17958E.description: An interconnectedness exists among the living and nonliving parts of an environment. This interconnectedness can be observed by the changes made by plants and animals in their environment.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Organisms and their environments are interconnected. Changes in one part of the system will affect other parts of the system.

F1AD67B0DFE40131590C68A86D17958E.description: People use the variety of plants and animals found throughout the world for food, clothing, and shelter (e.g., silk for clothing, wood for building shelters).

comments: Enduring Understanding: The development of technology has allowed us to apply our knowledge of genetics, reproduction, development and evolution to meet human needs and wants.

F1ACDBA0DFE40131590A68A86D17958E.description: Many different kinds of plants and animals live throughout the world. These plants and animals can be grouped according to the characteristics they share.

comments: Enduring Understanding: The diversity and changing of life forms over many generations is the result of natural selection, in which organisms with advantageous traits survive, reproduce, and pass those traits to offspring.

F1AC1DD0DFE40131590868A86D17958E.description: All plants and animals go through a life cycle of birth, growth, development, reproduction, and death. This cycle is predictable and describable, but differs from organism to organism.

F1ABCC90DFE40131590768A86D17958E.description: The offspring of some plants and animals do not resemble the parents. Similarities between parents and their offspring become more apparent as their life cycle continues (i.e., caterpillars become butterflies).

F1AB88F0DFE40131590668A86D17958E.description: The offspring of some plants and animals resemble the parents (i.e., a tree seedling resembles a mature tree).

comments: Enduring Understanding: Organisms reproduce, develop, have predictable life cycles, and pass on heritable traits to their offspring.

F1AB00E0DFE40131590468A86D17958E.description: Diversity and Continuity of Living Things

F1AABB00DFE40131590368A86D17958E.description: The ability of an organism to meet its needs for survival is dependent upon its environment. Manipulation of the environment can positively or negatively affect the well being of various organisms that live there.

F1AA6830DFE40131590268A86D17958E.description: Humans use devices and specialized equipment to ensure safety and to improve their quality of life (e.g., goggles, glasses, hearing aids, and wheelchairs).

F1AA13F0DFE40131590168A86D17958E.description: Technology expands the range of human senses.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Grades K-8: The life processes of organisms are affected by their interactions with each other and their environment, and may be altered by human manipulation. Grades 9-12: The health of humans and other organisms is affected by their interactions with each other and their environment, and may be altered by human manipulation.

F1A95960DFE4013158FF68A86D17958E.description: The brain receives signals from parts of the body via the senses. In response, the brain sends signals to parts of the body to influence reactions.

F1A91540DFE4013158FE68A86D17958E.description: Senses help humans and other organisms detect internal and external cues.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Organisms respond to internal and external cues, which allow them to survive.

F1A881D0DFE4013158FC68A86D17958E.description: In addition to basic needs for survival, living things have needs specific to the organism such as temperature range and food requirements.

F1A83F80DFE4013158FB68A86D17958E.description: Plants and animals are living things. All living things have basic needs for survival including air, water, food (nutrients), space, shelter, and light.

comments: Enduring Understanding: All organisms transfer matter and convert energy from one form to another. Both matter and energy are necessary to build and maintain structures within the organism.

F1A7B2C0DFE4013158F968A86D17958E.description: In animals the skeletal-muscular system provides structure, support and enables movement.

F1A76E30DFE4013158F868A86D17958E.description: Each plant or animal has different structures that serve different functions in growth, survival and reproduction.

F1A721E0DFE4013158F768A86D17958E.description: Plants and animals are similar to and different from each other in observable structures and behavior. These characteristics distinguish them from each other and from nonliving things.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Living systems, from the organismic to the cellular level, demonstrate the complementary nature of structure and function.

F1A61730DFE4013158F468A86D17958E.description: Weather can be observed, measured and described through the use of simple tools such as a thermometer, rain gauge and wind vane.

F1A5D640DFE4013158F368A86D17958E.description: Earth materials can be observed and described using simple tools (e.g., hand lens and balances).

comments: Enduring Understanding: Technology enables us to better understand Earth's systems. It also allows us to analyze the impact of human activities on Earth's systems and the impact of Earth's systems on human activity.

F1A53A60DFE4013158F168A86D17958E.description: Clouds are shaped by winds and are made of small water droplets or ice crystals. Cloud shapes can be used to help forecast weather.

F1A4F490DFE4013158F068A86D17958E.description: Water from rain, lakes, and underground, is needed by plants, animals and people for their everyday activities.

F1A4B150DFE4013158EF68A86D17958E.description: People who work or play outdoors often dress and base their activities on the speed of the wind and the temperature of the air.

F1A46D90DFE4013158EE68A86D17958E.description: Weather influences plants, animals and human activity.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Earth's components form systems. These systems continually interact at different rates of time, affecting the Earth locally and globally.

F1A3E0A0DFE4013158EC68A86D17958E.description: Rocks are natural combinations of minerals. Minerals can be classified according to their physical properties (i.e., luster, color and hardness).

F1A39830DFE4013158EB68A86D17958E.description: Soil type can be identified by testing for grain size and composition.

F1A345A0DFE4013158EA68A86D17958E.description: A soil's composition varies from environment to environment.

F1A30120DFE4013158E968A86D17958E.description: Sand, clay and humus have distinct physical properties and are components of soils.

F1A2BA20DFE4013158E868A86D17958E.description: Water can exist as a solid, liquid or gas and in different forms such as rain, snow and ice.

F1A26350DFE4013158E768A86D17958E.description: Components of Earth's system include minerals, rocks, soil, water and air. These materials can be observed, sorted and/or classified based on their physical properties.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Earth's systems can be broken down into individual components which have observable measurable properties.

F1A15920DFE4013158E468A86D17958E.description: Binoculars allow people to observe objects in the sky from Earth.

comments: Enduring Understandings: Grades K-5: Technology expands our knowledge of the Earth, Moon, and Sun System. Grades 6-8: Technology expands our knowledge of the Solar System. Grades 9-12: Technology expands our knowledge of the Universe.

F1A0C700DFE4013158E268A86D17958E.description: The appearance of the Moon changes in a cycle that takes about a month.

F1A084A0DFE4013158E168A86D17958E.description: The Moon can be observed sometimes at night and sometimes during the day.

F1A041A0DFE4013158E068A86D17958E.description: The pattern of day and night repeats every 24 hours. The Sun can only be seen in the daytime.

F19FF5F0DFE4013158DF68A86D17958E.description: The Sun and Moon appear to move slowly across the sky.

F19FA300DFE4013158DE68A86D17958E.description: From Earth many objects may be seen in the sky including the Sun, the Moon, stars, and man-made objects.

F19F59E0DFE4013158DD68A86D17958E.description: The shape of the Earth is similar to a sphere.

comments: Enduring Understanding: There are observable, predictable patterns of movement in the Sun, Earth, and Moon system that account for day/night.
Enduring Understanding for Grades 6-12: Observable, predictable patterns of movement in the Sun, Earth, Moon system occur because of gravitational interaction and energy from the Sun.

F19E89E0DFE4013158DA68A86D17958E.description: Moving air, moving water, and sunlight contain energy that can be put to our use.

comments: Enduring Understanding: People utilize a variety of resources to meet the basic and specific needs of life. Some of these resources cannot be replaced. Other resources can be replenished or exist in such vast quantities they are in no danger of becoming depleted. Often the energy stored in resources must be transformed into more useful forms and transported over great distances before it can be helpful to us.
F19E3DA0DFE4013158D968A86D17958E.description: The Production, Consumption and Application of Energy

F19DF1D0DFE4013158D868A86D17958E.description: When light hits an object, the light energy can become heat energy.

F19DAC50DFE4013158D768A86D17958E.description: Energy Interacting With Materials; the Transformation and Conservation of Energy
comments: Enduring Understanding: Energy readily transforms from one form to another, but these transformations are not always reversible. The details of these transformations depend upon the initial form of the energy and the properties of the materials involved. Energy may transfer into or out of a system and it may change forms, but the total energy cannot change.

F19D5D60DFE4013158D668A86D17958E.description: Transferring heat energy to an object will make it feel warmer by raising its temperature and it may cause a change in the object's physical properties.

F19D0BD0DFE4013158D568A86D17958E.description: Energy of a moving object can be transferred to other objects (i.e., the energy of moving water can be used to turn a waterwheel).

F19CBA70DFE4013158D468A86D17958E.description: When balanced forces act on an object it will remain at rest, but if unbalanced forces act on the object it will begin to move.

F19C6DE0DFE4013158D368A86D17958E.description: The position of an object gives its location relative to where you are (e.g., above, below, in front, or behind). The motion of an object describes how its position is changing. Pushing or pulling on an object can change its position or motion.

F19C1500DFE4013158D268A86D17958E.description: Forces and the Transfer of Energy
comments: Enduring Understanding: Changes take place because of the transfer of energy. Energy is transferred to matter through the action of forces. Different forces are responsible for the transfer of the different forms of energy.

F19BCDA0DFE4013158D168A86D17958E.description: Electrical energy is a form of energy that is used to operate many of our tools and appliances.

F19B7650DFE4013158D068A86D17958E.description: Heat energy is a form of energy that makes things warmer.

F19B0920DFE4013158CF68A86D17958E.description: Objects that move (i.e., moving air, moving water) have energy because of their motion.

F19ABE90DFE4013158CE68A86D17958E.description: The Sun is a source of energy that lights and warms the Earth.

F19A6CF0DFE4013158CD68A86D17958E.description: The Forms and Sources of Energy
comments: Enduring Understanding: Energy takes many forms. These forms can be grouped into types of energy that are associated with the motion of mass (kinetic energy), and types of energy associated with the position of mass and with energy fields (potential energy).

F199E5D0DFE4013158CB68A86D17958E.description: Technology has created new materials that can help people solve problems.

F199A040DFE4013158CA68A86D17958E.description: The properties of materials influence their use. Some materials are more suitable for making a particular product or device.

comments: Enduring Understanding: People develop new materials as a response to the needs of society and the pursuit of knowledge. This development may have risks and benefits to humans and the environment.

F1990C30DFE4013158C868A86D17958E.description: Physical properties of materials can be changed by exposure to water, heat, light, or by cutting, mixing, and grinding.

F198B700DFE4013158C768A86D17958E.description: Materials exist in one of three states – solid, liquid, or gas. Solids and liquids have easily observable properties and may change from one form to the other.

F1986E60DFE4013158C668A86D17958E.description: Materials can be described and classified according to the following physical properties: size, shape, mass, texture, color, and material composition. Students can observe materials' physical properties by using tools that include rulers, balances, thermometers and hand lenses.

comments: Enduring Understanding: The structures of materials determine their properties.

F1977540DFE4013158C368A86D17958E.description: Much has been learned about the natural world but there is still much to understand.

F1972E50DFE4013158C268A86D17958E.description: People from all parts of the world practice science and make many important scientific contributions.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Understanding past processes and contributions is essential in building scientific knowledge.

F1969E60DFE4013158C068A86D17958E.description: Tools are useful in science to help gather data for observations and measurements and provide a safe means of conducting an investigation.

F1965CB0DFE4013158BF68A86D17958E.description: People have invented new technologies to solve problems.

comments: Enduring Understanding: The development of technology and advancement in science influence and drive each other forward.

F195C490DFE4013158BD68A86D17958E.description: The use of mathematics, reading, writing, and technology are important in conducting scientific inquiries.

F1955E20DFE4013158BC68A86D17958E.description: The purpose of communicating with others is to share evidence and conclusions. Scientists communicate the results of their investigations to others.

F194FF60DFE4013158BB68A86D17958E.description: Scientists use observations from investigations and knowledge that is already known to develop an explanation.

F194B510DFE4013158BA68A86D17958E.description: The purpose of accurate observations and data collection is to provide evidence. Scientists use tools to enhance their senses in order to obtain more evidence.

F1946970DFE4013158B968A86D17958E.description: In a science investigation, a fair test is one in which all of the conditions are kept constant except the one condition being investigated.

F1941FD0DFE4013158B868A86D17958E.description: Scientific investigations, whether conducted by students or scientists, involve asking a question about the natural world.

F193D8F0DFE4013158B768A86D17958E.description: Understandings and Abilities of Scientific Inquiry
comments: Enduring Understanding: Scientific inquiry involves asking scientifically-oriented questions, collecting evidence, forming explanations, connecting explanations to scientific knowledge and theory, and communicating and justifying the explanation.

F1938AA0DFE4013158B668A86D17958E.description: Nature and Application of Science and Technology

166617BC34924735B45784D59FDFEF2A.description: Recognize that trees are replanted in an attempt to replace those that are cut down.

79DC39A5DABA4DCCA47160DB9482382B.description: Humans can alter the living and non-living factors within an ecosystem, thereby creating changes to the overall system.

38220D23A070444DBF98ADD7CA8F3A3D.description: Recognize that sunlight is needed by plants for energy.

BF2094A4F6E74C8BBC44323237DD8748.description: Matter needed to sustain life is continually recycled among and between organisms and the environment. Energy from the sun flows irreversibly through ecosystems and is conserved as organisms use and transform it.

A64CA6F4B45944769E52DD7169AB1B8C.description: Recognize that animals use plants in a variety of ways (e.g., shelter, food and protection).

CFDAB335E98C403DB8B29804C725FE69.description: Identify ways in which living organisms interact with each other and their environment (e.g., birds nest in trees, birds eat worms).

7C1EDA29D1C64BAC9986D376CC3AD84C.description: Recognize that humans interact with the environment through the use of their five senses.

025AD09C31154190BC45CDE2293EF9CE.description: Organisms and their environments are interconnected. Changes in one part of the system will affect other parts of the system.

EFDC8C90DFE40131551068A86D17958E.description: Identify and list the many different ways in which trees are used by people to meet human wants and needs (i.e., food, shelter, shade, paper products, wood for fuel, furniture, etc.).

EFDC44C0DFE40131550F68A86D17958E.description: The development of technology has allowed us to apply our knowledge of genetics, reproduction, development and evolution to meet human wants and needs.

EFDBFCB0DFE40131550E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that there are many different kinds of trees in the world. While there are many similarities and differences among the trees, they are all trees.

EFDBB3B0DFE40131550D68A86D17958E.description: The diversity and changing of life forms over many generations is the result of natural selection, in which organisms with advantageous traits survive, reproduce, and pass those traits to offspring.

EFDB6720DFE40131550C68A86D17958E.description: Construct, through the use of pictorials, the life cycle of a tree. Describe the tree in different stages of its life cycle.

EFB80550DFE40131550B68A86D17958E.description: Realize that organisms reproduce organisms of the same kind (e.g., dogs have puppies).

EFB7C0E0DFE40131550A68A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe similarities and differences between parents and offspring (e.g., roots on a mature tree vs. roots on a seedling). Use a hand lens (magnifier) as an appropriate instrument for observing in closer detail.

EFB77BE0DFE40131550968A86D17958E.description: Organisms reproduce, develop, have predictable life cycles, and pass on heritable traits to their offspring.

EFB732D0DFE40131550868A86D17958E.description: Diversity and Continuity of Living Things

EFB6DD50DFE40131550768A86D17958E.description: Describe how the senses can be protected when conducting scientific investigations, e.g. goggles protect eyes, gloves protect hands.

EFB682C0DFE40131550668A86D17958E.description: The life processes of organisms are affected by their interactions with each other and their environment, and may be altered by human manipulation.

EFB63830DFE40131550568A86D17958E.description: Observe how the living things in an environment change with the seasons (e.g., trees lose their leaves in the winter).

EFB5E9F0DFE40131550468A86D17958E.description: Describe how the five senses help humans react to their environment, (e.g., hear a whistle and lineup, feel cold air and put on a jacket).

EFB5A290DFE40131550368A86D17958E.description: Organisms respond to internal external cues, which allow them to survive.

EFB55460DFE40131550268A86D17958E.description: Identify the basic needs that plants and animals need to survive including light, air, water, and nutrients.

EFB4F080DFE40131550168A86D17958E.description: All organisms transfer matter and convert energy from one form to another. Both matter and energy are necessary to build and maintain structures within the organism.

EFB49510DFE40131550068A86D17958E.description: Identify structures on plants and animals and describe how the structure functions (e.g., trees have bark for protection and rabbits have fur to keep them warm).

EFB452D0DFE4013154FF68A86D17958E.description: Use non-standard units of measure to compare the size and mass of structures of living things (e.g., string around trees, paper clips to measure length of leaves).

EFB40F80DFE4013154FE68A86D17958E.description: Use a hand lens (magnifier) to inspect a variety of living things and demonstrate through discussion and drawings how the lens extends the sense of sight to see structures in greater detail.

EFB3CF80DFE4013154FD68A86D17958E.description: Sort, group, and regroup a variety of familiar living and non-living things based on their physical properties (e.g., shape, color, texture, taste, size, etc.).

EFB38F70DFE4013154FC68A86D17958E.description: Use the physical properties of living and non-living things to describe their similarities and differences.

718520E28E1D44D28A0010FA9AC501B9.description: Students will understand how to evaluate financial products and services to minimize financial risks.

comments: Risks are associated with life and unplanned events can have serious or catastrophic financial consequences over which an individual may have little control. A citizen with the knowledge and skills to evaluate financial products can prevent or limit loss.

06768B49BACE4C95933FEC0A7D49539D.description: Students will evaluate the costs and benefits of major savings and investing options.

97824952197A4F69BDEC178925B2B4E2.description: Students will demonstrate that personal savings and investment compound over time and contribute to meeting financial goals.

comments: Every savings and investment decision has a trade-off in terms of giving up goods and services today. Savings options and investments vary in their potential risks, liquidity, and rate of return. Individuals and households invest by purchasing assets that may earn income and/or appreciate in value over time.

C51B647BB28D41E1917AA52B451F6D9E.description: Students will examine how ability to pay and personal credit history influences an individual's financial opportunities and choices.

05E8C1DA7A48417E8FACAEDE5F1285E5.description: Students will analyze the benefits and costs of various payment options while applying the mechanics of money management.

comments: When purchasing goods and services, individuals must choose among payment options to maximize benefits. Prudent individuals limit borrowing based on their ability to repay.

10AFFE18A33F4585A6EAF76F11190DBA.description: Students will create an overall financial plan for spending and saving in order to achieve personal goals.

B7734F6D88C34D86AEAC78B8383A964C.description: Students will apply problem-solving strategies and cost benefit analysis to assess the consequences of financial decisions.

comments: An individual's goals affect how they value the benefits and costs of alternative choices. A financial plan is a strategy to accomplish an individual's or household's financial goals that will change as an individual's or household's situation changes. Effective financial plans incorporate the possibility of unexpected expenditures.
