DFCDCCC0DFE4013136B468A86D17958E.description: Notate symbols and terms referring to dynamics, tempo and articulation

DFCD4070DFE4013136B268A86D17958E.description: Notate symbols and terms for meter and rhythm

DFCCF530DFE4013136B168A86D17958E.description: Read a single line of an instrumental or vocal part

DFCC0B30DFE4013136AE68A86D17958E.description: Identify and define standard notation symbols

DFCB6BF0DFE4013136AC68A86D17958E.description: Compose short songs and instrumental pieces

DFCB2530DFE4013136AB68A86D17958E.description: Composing and arranging music within specific guidelines

DFCADB50DFE4013136AA68A86D17958E.description: Improvise melodies over given rhythm and tonal context

DFCA9E20DFE4013136A968A86D17958E.description: Improvise rhythmically with voice or on instrument

DFC84910DFE4013136A068A86D17958E.description: Perform in groups with blend and balance

DFC80C50DFE40131369F68A86D17958E.description: Perform music representing diverse genres and styles

DFCA2310DFE4013136A768A86D17958E.description: Perform an independent part in an ensemble setting

DFC9E460DFE4013136A668A86D17958E.description: Perform in groups in response to gestures of a conductor

DFC956F0DFE4013136A468A86D17958E.description: Perform with proper posture and breathing

DFC8FE80DFE4013136A368A86D17958E.description: Perform melodies by ear using a melodic instrument

DFC88530DFE4013136A168A86D17958E.description: Perform on pitched and unpitched instruments in rhythm while applying a steady beat

DFC7CF20DFE40131369E68A86D17958E.description: Imitate rhythmic and melodic patterns on pitched and unpitched instruments

DFC78B50DFE40131369D68A86D17958E.description: Performing on instruments independently and with others a varied repertoire of music

DFC52FD0DFE40131369468A86D17958E.description: Sing a repertoire of choral literature with expression and technical accuracy including songs performed from memory

DFC4E780DFE40131369368A86D17958E.description: Sing expressively with phrasing, dynamics and stylistic interpretation

DFC4A330DFE40131369268A86D17958E.description: Sing a repertoire of songs representing different genres, styles and languages

DFC74580DFE40131369C68A86D17958E.description: Sing in groups in response to gestures of a conductor

DFC68FF0DFE40131369968A86D17958E.description: Sing expressively utilizing dynamics and phrasing

DFC61050DFE40131369768A86D17958E.description: Sing demonstrating proper posture and breathing

DFC5CA30DFE40131369668A86D17958E.description: Sing on pitch in rhythm while applying a steady beat

DFC57960DFE40131369568A86D17958E.description: Sing on pitch within the appropriate singing range

DFC40840DFE40131369068A86D17958E.description: Singing independently and with others, a varied repertoire of music.

F3291600DFE401315B4168A86D17958E.description: Students will analyze and interpret the influence of the distribution of the world's resources, political stability, national efforts to encourage or discourage trade, and the flow of investment on patterns of international trade.

F328D060DFE401315B4068A86D17958E.description: Students will examine the patterns and results of international trade [International trade].

F3288D70DFE401315B3F68A86D17958E.description: Students will analyze the wide range of opportunities and consequences resulting from the current transitions from command to market economies in many countries.

F3284FD0DFE401315B3E68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand different types of economic systems and how they change [Economic systems].

F3281060DFE401315B3D68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop an understanding of how economies function as a whole, including the causes and effects of inflation, unemployment, business cycles, and monetary and fiscal policies.

F327CFE0DFE401315B3C68A86D17958E.description: Students will examine the interaction of individuals, families, communities, businesses, and governments in a market economy [Macroeconomics].

F32787D0DFE401315B3B68A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate how individual economic choices are made within the context of a market economy in which markets influence the production and distribution of goods and services.

F32735D0DFE401315B3A68A86D17958E.description: Students will analyze the potential costs and benefits of personal economic choices in a market economy [Microeconomics].

F204C3C0DFE40131598568A86D17958E.description: Different technologies are used to access resources to meet human wants and needs. In many cases the environment is affected and resources become limited. Some activities may include burning of fossil fuels, logging, building of highways, shopping centers, and dams, introduction of one species to control another species, spraying of insects, as well as some aspects of farming.

F2047D30DFE40131598468A86D17958E.description: Human activities may cause pollution of air, water and soil.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Humans can alter the living and non-living factors within an ecosystem, thereby creating changes to the overall system.

F203E270DFE40131598268A86D17958E.description: Dead plants and animals are broken down by decomposers.

F20394C0DFE40131598168A86D17958E.description: Animals eat plants or other animals that have eaten plants. Animals obtain energy and materials for body repair and growth from food.

F20340C0DFE40131598068A86D17958E.description: Plants need energy from the Sun, water and nutrients for growth and survival.

F202EEF0DFE40131597F68A86D17958E.description: Energy Flow and Material Cycles in the Environment
comments: Enduring Understandings: Matter needed to sustain life is continually recycled among and between organisms and the environment. Energy from the Sun flows irreversibly through ecosystems and is conserved as organisms use and transform it.

F2028C40DFE40131597E68A86D17958E.description: In order to survive, populations within an ecosystem require a balance of resources.

F2023310DFE40131597D68A86D17958E.description: Changes in an organism's environment may be either beneficial or harmful. Organisms may be affected by other organisms, by various physical factors (e.g., rainfall, temperature), by physical forces (e.g., storms, earthquakes), and by daily, seasonal, and annual cycles.

F201E370DFE40131597C68A86D17958E.description: Adaptations in organisms enable them to live and reproduce in certain environments. Those organisms that are best suited for a particular environment have adaptations that allow them to compete for available resources and cope with the physical conditions of their immediate surroundings.

F2019AE0DFE40131597B68A86D17958E.description: All living organisms interact with the living and nonliving parts of their surroundings to meet their needs for survival. These interactions lead to a constant exchange of matter.

F20156A0DFE40131597A68A86D17958E.description: People depend on living and nonliving resources to satisfy their need for food, shelter, and fuel.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Organisms and their environments are interconnected. Changes in one part of the system will affect other parts of the system.

F20071D0DFE40131597768A86D17958E.description: Through the use of biotechnology, scientists engineer plants and manipulate growing conditions to meet human needs and wants (e.g., fruits without seeds, hydroponics).

comments: Enduring Understanding: The development of technology has allowed us to apply our knowledge of genetics, reproduction, development and evolution to meet human needs and wants.

F1FFEBB0DFE40131597568A86D17958E.description: Organisms of the same type vary in appearance. These variations may provide an advantage in reproduction and survival.

comments: Enduring Understanding: The diversity and changing of life forms over many generations is the result of natural selection, in which organisms with advantageous traits survive, reproduce, and pass those traits to offspring.

F1FF6260DFE40131597368A86D17958E.description: Most plants go through a life cycle of germination, growth, development, reproduction, and death.

F1FF0AE0DFE40131597268A86D17958E.description: An organism's physical appearance can change without the change being passed on to its offspring (e.g., dyed hair, loss of a claw).

F1FEC490DFE40131597168A86D17958E.description: Physical characteristics are passed on from parent to offspring. Organisms with two parents inherit characteristics of both.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Organisms reproduce, develop, have predictable life cycles, and pass on heritable traits to their offspring.

F1FE2620DFE40131596F68A86D17958E.description: Diversity and Continuity of Living Things

F1FDD400DFE40131596E68A86D17958E.description: Short term and long term studies are used to determine the effects of environmental changes (natural and man-made) on the health of the organisms within that environment.

F1FD7BB0DFE40131596D68A86D17958E.description: The development of safety devices and protective equipment has helped in the prevention of injuries.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Grades K-8: The life processes of organisms are affected by their interactions with each other and their environment, and may be altered by human manipulation. Grades 9-12: The health of humans and other organisms is affected by their interactions with each other and their environment, and may be altered by human manipulation.

F1FCE4F0DFE40131596B68A86D17958E.description: There are similarities and differences in how organisms respond to internal and external cues. These behaviors may include strategies for acquiring food, building shelters, or evading predators.

F1FCA020DFE40131596A68A86D17958E.description: An organism displays behaviors in response to internal cues, such as hunger, and external cues, such as light, temperature, or interaction with living things.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Organisms respond to internal and external cues, which allow them to survive.

F1FBE700DFE40131596868A86D17958E.description: Animals need food to provide materials and energy for life which they derive directly or indirectly from plants.

F1FB8550DFE40131596768A86D17958E.description: Plants need the Sun's energy to grow and survive.

comments: Enduring Understanding: All organisms transfer matter and convert energy from one form to another. Both matter and energy are necessary to build and maintain structures within the organism.

F1FAF4B0DFE40131596568A86D17958E.description: Organisms can be grouped based on similarities and differences in their structures and functions. These may include characteristics such as appendages, roots and leaves of plants, or the presence or lack of a backbone.

F1FAAA30DFE40131596468A86D17958E.description: The digestive system has major structures that function to break down food for use in the body. The major parts of the digestive system include the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine.

F1FA57A0DFE40131596368A86D17958E.description: Structures that function for similar purposes in living things may have different appearances.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Living systems, from the organismic to the cellular level, demonstrate the complementary nature of structure and function.

F1F95570DFE40131596068A86D17958E.description: Some satellites allow scientists to observe, over time, large-scale changes in the geosphere as well as the development of short term weather events.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Technology enables us to better understand Earth's systems. It also allows us to analyze the impact of human activities on Earth's systems and the impact of Earth's systems on human activity.

F1F8AE30DFE40131595E68A86D17958E.description: Local weather at any point in time varies at different locations around the world.

F1F86220DFE40131595D68A86D17958E.description: Some weather events, such as snowstorms, hurricanes, thunderstorms or tornadoes are more likely to occur at different times of the year.

F1F816F0DFE40131595C68A86D17958E.description: Weather changes daily and seasonally. Weather in Delaware may change little from day to day, but can vary greatly when storm systems move into the area.

F1F7CD10DFE40131595B68A86D17958E.description: The surface of Earth changes constantly. Some of these changes happen slowly and are difficult to detect on a daily basis. Other changes happen quickly and result from events (i.e., major storms and volcanoes).

F1F76790DFE40131595A68A86D17958E.description: Water in rivers and streams transports materials. As a general rule, when a stream enters a larger body of water, less massive materials in suspension will travel farther than more massive materials before settling.

F1F70670DFE40131595968A86D17958E.description: The flow of water can be affected by human activities, ground cover and the slope of the land affected.

F1F6BD90DFE40131595868A86D17958E.description: Water reshapes Earth's land surface by eroding rock and soil in some areas and depositing them in other areas.

F1F66060DFE40131595768A86D17958E.description: Earth is a dynamic system resulting from interactions among the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Earth's components form systems. These systems continually interact at different rates of time, affecting the Earth locally and globally.

F1F5C700DFE40131595568A86D17958E.description: The ability of water to pass through soil depends on the relative amounts of clay and sand in the soil.

F1F58560DFE40131595468A86D17958E.description: Rocks and minerals are broken down over time to clay and sand sized particles. These particles combine with plant remains to form soil.

F1F54350DFE40131595368A86D17958E.description: Water exists in three states (solid, liquid and gas) that are dependent upon the surrounding temperature.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Earth's systems can be broken down into individual components which have observable measurable properties.

F1F46AC0DFE40131595068A86D17958E.description: Terrestrial telescopes allow people to observe objects in the sky from Earth.

F1F42740DFE40131594F68A86D17958E.description: Humanity's view of the Solar System has expanded enormously as a result of our exploration of outer space. The Hubble telescope gives us a better view of the many planets than the view we have from the Earth. Robot probes, sent to planets, send back close-up pictures of their surfaces.

comments: Enduring Understandings: Grades K-5: Technology expands our knowledge of the Earth, Moon, and Sun System. Grades 6-8: Technology expands our knowledge of the Solar System. Grades 9-12: Technology expands our knowledge of the Universe.

F1F39A90DFE40131594D68A86D17958E.description: Earth is one of the planets in our Solar System that orbits the Sun. The Sun we see during the day is our nearest star. Stars we see at night lie outside our Solar System.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Grades 4-5: Earth is part of a system that includes other planets.
Most objects in the Solar System orbit the Sun and have distinctive physical characteristics and orderly motion (grades 6-8) which are a result of their formation and changes over time (grades 9-11).

F1F2EA20DFE40131594B68A86D17958E.description: The Sun is much larger than the Moon. Although the Moon is closer to Earth than the Sun, the two appear to be the same size when viewed from Earth. This is because objects appear smaller as the distance from the viewer increases.

F1F2A5C0DFE40131594A68A86D17958E.description: The Moon orbits the Earth. The appearance of the Moon changes as it moves through its orbit. These changes are called phases.

F1F26240DFE40131594968A86D17958E.description: The cycle from day to night is caused by the Earth's rotation. Earth undergoes one complete rotation about every 24 hours.

F1F21D30DFE40131594868A86D17958E.description: The apparent path of the Sun, as seen from Earth, is from east to west. Over the course of a day, half of the Earth is always illuminated by the Sun causing day, and the half not illuminated by the Sun experiences nighttime.

comments: Enduring Understanding: There are observable, predictable patterns of movement in the Sun, Earth, and Moon system that account for day/night.
Enduring Understanding for Grades 6-12: Observable, predictable patterns of movement in the Sun, Earth, Moon system occur because of gravitational interaction and energy from the Sun.

F1F13C40DFE40131594568A86D17958E.description: The production of most of the energy that we use in our daily lives comes from energy stored in natural resources. The quantity of these resources is limited, so it is important to conserve our natural resources by using them wisely.

F1F0DFE0DFE40131594468A86D17958E.description: The Production, Consumption and Application of Energy
comments: Enduring Understanding: People utilize a variety of resources to meet the basic and specific needs of life. Some of these resources cannot be replaced. Other resources can be replenished or exist in such vast quantities they are in no danger of becoming depleted. Often the energy stored in resources must be transformed into more useful forms and transported over great distances before it can be helpful to us.

F1F084C0DFE40131594368A86D17958E.description: Electrical energy in circuits can be changed (transformed) into light, heat, sound, and the energy of motion.

F1F01860DFE40131594268A86D17958E.description: When light is absorbed by a material, most of its energy is changed (transformed) into heat energy. Heat energy can also be produced by electrical and mechanical machines and by one object rubbing against another object.

F1EFD520DFE40131594168A86D17958E.description: When light strikes an object, the light can reflect off of its surface or pass into the object. The light that passes into the object can pass through it or be absorbed by the material that makes up the object. Light usually refracts when passing from one material into another.

F1EF8E40DFE40131594068A86D17958E.description: Energy Interacting With Materials; the Transformation and Conservation of Energy
comments: Enduring Understanding: Energy readily transforms from one form to another, but these transformations are not always reversible. The details of these transformations depend upon the initial form of the energy and the properties of the materials involved. Energy may transfer into or out of a system and it may change forms, but the total energy cannot change.

F1EF43D0DFE40131593F68A86D17958E.description: Some materials are magnetic and can be pushed or pulled by other magnets.

F1EEF400DFE40131593E68A86D17958E.description: Some materials allow electricity to flow freely (conductors), while other materials inhibit the flow of electricity (insulators).

F1EEB0A0DFE40131593D68A86D17958E.description: The energy of electricity is transferred to electrical devices through simple closed circuits (simple series or simple parallel circuits).

F1EE6CF0DFE40131593C68A86D17958E.description: The transfer of heat energy may produce changes in the state of a substance.

F1EE2690DFE40131593B68A86D17958E.description: Pushing and pulling forces can be used to transfer energy from one object to another.

F1EDDB90DFE40131593A68A86D17958E.description: A force must be applied to change the speed of a moving object or change its direction of motion. Larger forces will create greater changes in an object's speed in a given unit of time.

F1ED9130DFE40131593968A86D17958E.description: The speeds of two or more objects can be compared (i.e., faster, slower) by measuring the distance traveled in a given unit of time, or by measuring the time needed to travel a fixed distance.

F1ED3A60DFE40131593868A86D17958E.description: Force is any push or pull exerted by one object on another. Some forces (e.g., magnetic forces and gravity) can make things move without touching them.

F1ECF360DFE40131593768A86D17958E.description: Forces and the Transfer of Energy
comments: Enduring Understanding: Changes take place because of the transfer of energy. Energy is transferred to matter through the action of forces. Different forces are responsible for the transfer of the different forms of energy.

F1ECAFE0DFE40131593668A86D17958E.description: The energy obtained from electrical outlets is electrical energy that was produced at an electrical power plant. Electrical energy can be generated and then transmitted over great distances. Batteries are portable sources of electrical energy.

F1EC6390DFE40131593568A86D17958E.description: Heat energy raises the object's temperature or changes the state of the object (i.e., solid to liquid, liquid to gas).

F1EC1390DFE40131593468A86D17958E.description: Sound is a form of energy that is produced by vibrating objects, and can be described by its pitch and its loudness (volume). Sound travels faster through some substances than others.

F1EBBBE0DFE40131593368A86D17958E.description: Energy can be stored in an elastic material when it is stretched.

F1EB5A00DFE40131593268A86D17958E.description: The energy of a moving object depends on its speed. Faster moving objects have more energy than slower moving objects.

F1EB1450DFE40131593168A86D17958E.description: Energy from the sun includes visible light, which consists of a combination of different colored light, and components that are not visible, which include infrared and ultraviolet light waves.

F1EAC100DFE40131593068A86D17958E.description: The Forms and Sources of Energy
comments: Enduring Understanding: Energy takes many forms. These forms can be grouped into types of energy that are associated with the motion of mass (kinetic energy), and types of energy associated with the position of mass and with energy fields (potential energy).

F1EA11C0DFE40131592E68A86D17958E.description: Many materials can be recycled and used again (sometimes in different forms).

comments: Enduring Understanding: People develop new materials as a response to the needs of society and the pursuit of knowledge. This development may have risks and benefits to humans and the environment.

F1E97370DFE40131592C68A86D17958E.description: The mass of an object remains unchanged when broken into parts. The sum of the parts equals the whole.

comments: Enduring Understanding: When materials interact within a closed system, the total mass of the system remains the same.

F1E8EC70DFE40131592A68A86D17958E.description: When a solid is dissolved in a liquid, a solution is formed that can be separated through the process of evaporation.

F1E8A860DFE40131592968A86D17958E.description: Physical properties can be used to separate mixtures through techniques such as filtration and evaporation.

F1E85EC0DFE40131592868A86D17958E.description: Mixtures can consist of different combinations of solids and/or liquids. The characteristics of these resulting mixtures depend on the relative amounts and properties of the components.

F1E80C90DFE40131592768A86D17958E.description: Most materials are physical mixtures. Physical mixtures can be composed of different kinds of materials, each having distinct physical properties. These physical property differences can be used to separate, sort, and group the materials of the mixture.

comments: Enduring Understanding: The properties of a mixture are based on the properties of its components.

F1E77EF0DFE40131592568A86D17958E.description: Heating and cooling of materials may produce changes in the state of solids, liquids and gases.

F1E72F90DFE40131592468A86D17958E.description: Observable physical properties can be used to classify materials. These physical properties may include solubility, mass, magnetism, and electrical conductivity. Tools such as graduated cylinders, balances, rulers, magnifiers, simple circuits, and magnets are used to study the physical properties.

comments: Enduring Understanding: The structures of materials determine their properties.

F1E636B0DFE40131592168A86D17958E.description: Contributions by individuals have been essential in advancing the body of scientific knowledge.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Understanding past processes and contributions is essential in building scientific knowledge.

F1E5ACA0DFE40131591F68A86D17958E.description: Science and technology are related. Technology provides the tools needed for science to investigate questions and may provide solutions to society's problems, wants, or needs. Not all technological solutions are effective, uniformly beneficial, or equally available to everyone.

comments: Enduring Understanding: The development of technology and advancement in science influence and drive each other forward.

F1E51EA0DFE40131591D68A86D17958E.description: The use of mathematics, reading, writing, and technology are important in conducting scientific inquiries.

F1E4CEB0DFE40131591C68A86D17958E.description: The purpose of communicating is to share and justify results. Scientists communicate their results to others, including the details that allow others to replicate the results.

F1E47700DFE40131591B68A86D17958E.description: The body of scientific knowledge grows as scientists ask questions, conduct investigations, develop explanations and compare results with what is already known.

F1E42F50DFE40131591A68A86D17958E.description: The purpose of accurate data collection is to provide evidence to compare with the prediction.

F1E3E230DFE40131591968A86D17958E.description: Fair test design supports the validity of the investigation. Sometimes it is not possible to know everything that will have an effect on the investigation or control all conditions.

F1E399C0DFE40131591868A86D17958E.description: Scientific investigations involve asking a focused scientific question. Investigations differ depending upon the question being asked.

comments: Enduring Understanding: Scientific inquiry involves asking scientifically-oriented questions, collecting evidence, forming explanations, connecting explanations to scientific knowledge and theory, and communicating and justifying the explanation.
F1E351E0DFE40131591768A86D17958E.description: Understandings and Abilities of Scientific Inquiry

F1E304A0DFE40131591668A86D17958E.description: Nature and Application of Science and Technology

document.title: Delaware Dance Content Standards and Grade Level Expectations

E1297ED0DFE40131398768A86D17958E.description: Observe dance, both live and recorded on video; compare and contrast the aesthetic impact of the two observations through writing

E1293D60DFE40131398668A86D17958E.description: Create a project that reveals similarities and differences between the arts

E128F910DFE40131398568A86D17958E.description: Create a dance project that reveals understanding of a concept or idea from another discipline (e.g., poetry, physics, geometry)

E128AA70DFE40131398468A86D17958E.description: Respond to a dance using another art form; explain the connections between the dance and their response to it (such as stating how their paintings reflect the dance they saw)

E1286EB0DFE40131398368A86D17958E.description: Making connections between dance and other disciplines

E12832B0DFE40131398268A86D17958E.description: Explain how healthy practices (such as nutrition, safety) enhance ability to dance, citing multiple examples

E127F6B0DFE40131398168A86D17958E.description: Making connections between dance and healthful living

E127BA00DFE40131398068A86D17958E.description: Perform folk dances from various cultures

E1277300DFE40131397F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating and understanding dance in various cultures and historical periods

E1272C60DFE40131397E68A86D17958E.description: Explore, discover and realize multiple solutions to a given movement problem; choose their favorite solution and discuss the reasons for that choice

E126CEC0DFE40131397D68A86D17958E.description: Observe two dances and discuss (compare and contrast) how they are similar and different in terms of one of the compositional elements (e.g., space, time, force/energy)

E1268C70DFE40131397C68A86D17958E.description: Observe and discuss how dance is different from other forms of human movement (e.g., sports, everyday gestures)

E1264CE0DFE40131397B68A86D17958E.description: Discuss how skills developed in dance are applicable to a variety of careers

E1260900DFE40131397A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate appropriate audience behavior in watching dance performances; discuss their opinions about the dances with their peers in a supportive and constructive way

E125C770DFE40131397968A86D17958E.description: Applying and demonstrating critical and creative thinking skills in dance

E1258500DFE40131397868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the difference between pantomiming and abstracting a gesture

E1253AE0DFE40131397768A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and/or explain how lighting and costuming can contribute to the meaning of a dance

E124E0A0DFE40131397668A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain how different accompaniment (such as sound, music, spoken text) can affect the meaning of a dance

E1249390DFE40131397568A86D17958E.description: Take an active role in a class discussion about interpretations of and reactions to a dance

E1244F30DFE40131397468A86D17958E.description: Understanding dance as a way to create and communicate meaning

E123FE60DFE40131397368A86D17958E.description: Create and perform a phrase utilizing compositional elements (e.g., space, time, force/energy)

E123BB10DFE40131397268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate structures or forms (e.g., AB, ABA, canon, call and response, narrative, palindrome, theme and variation, rondo, round, contemporary forms) through brief dance studies

E12366E0DFE40131397168A86D17958E.description: Create and identify the sequential parts of a dance phrase (e.g., beginning, middle, and end)

E1231380DFE40131397068A86D17958E.description: Use improvisation to generate movement for choreography

E122D670DFE40131396F68A86D17958E.description: Improvise, create and perform dances based on original ideas and concepts from other sources

E1229960DFE40131396E68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate basic partner skills (e.g., copying, leading and following, mirroring)

E1225B60DFE40131396D68A86D17958E.description: Understanding choreographic principles, processes and structures

E1221CD0DFE40131396C68A86D17958E.description: Execute techniques from different genres/styles (e.g. ballet, modern dance, jazz, tap, multi-cultural)

E121DF40DFE40131396B68A86D17958E.description: Memorize and reproduce extended movement sequences

E1219B10DFE40131396A68A86D17958E.description: Transfer spatial patterns from the visual to the kinesthetic

E1214B70DFE40131396968A86D17958E.description: Execute basic movement phrases individually and in a group

E1210CD0DFE40131396868A86D17958E.description: Explain and execute the underlying principles of movement skill (e.g., alignment, balance, initiation of movement, articulation of isolated body parts, weight shift, elevation and landing, fall and recovery)

E120CE10DFE40131396768A86D17958E.description: Transfer rhythmic patterns from the aural to the kinesthetic

E1208CD0DFE40131396668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate eight basic locomotor movements (e.g., walk, run, hop, jump, leap, gallop, slide, skip) traveling forward, backward, sideward, diagonally, turning

E1204930DFE40131396568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate accuracy in moving to a musical beat and responding to changes in tempo

E1200320DFE40131396468A86D17958E.description: Perform axial movements (e.g., bend, stretch, twist, turn, swing, collapse)

E11FAB80DFE40131396368A86D17958E.description: Identifying and demonstrating movement elements and skills in performing arts

F094B140DFE40131569C68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that fossils indicate that many organisms that lived long ago are extinct. Use index fossils to determine the relative age of rock sequences, and environmental conditions at the time of formation. Recognize, through fossil evidence, that some species can be traced back in geologic time.

F0945F40DFE40131569B68A86D17958E.description: The diversity and changing of life forms over many generations is the result of natural selection, in which organisms with advantageous traits survive, reproduce, and pass those traits to offspring.

F093FFC0DFE40131569A68A86D17958E.description: Diversity and Continuity of Living Things

F093B1B0DFE40131569968A86D17958E.description: Research and report on how body systems are affected by lifestyle choices such as diet or exercise, for example lack of exercise leads to cardiovascular disease.

F0936A30DFE40131569868A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of human body systems to synthesize research data and make informed decisions regarding personal and public health.

F09326B0DFE40131569768A86D17958E.description: The life processes of organisms are affected by their interactions with each other and their environment, and may be altered by human manipulation.

F092CCD0DFE40131569668A86D17958E.description: Conduct simple investigations (how the body reacts to exercise, changes in temperature, etc.) to determine how the systems in the human organism respond to various external stimuli to maintain stable internal conditions.

F09263D0DFE40131569568A86D17958E.description: Organisms respond to internal external cues, which allow them to survive.

F0920570DFE40131569468A86D17958E.description: Trace how the circulatory, respiratory, and digestive systems interact to transport the food and oxygen required to provide energy for life processes.

F091C400DFE40131569368A86D17958E.description: All organisms transfer matter and convert energy from one form to another. Both matter and energy are necessary to build and maintain structures within the organism.

F0918260DFE40131569268A86D17958E.description: Express how the human circulatory, respiratory, and digestive systems work together to carry out life processes.

F0914040DFE40131569168A86D17958E.description: Label and describe the functions of the basic parts of the digestive tract including the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, liver, large intestine (colon), rectum and anus.

F090FD40DFE40131569068A86D17958E.description: Label and describe the functions of the basic parts of the respiratory system including the trachea, bronchi and lungs.

F090B510DFE40131568F68A86D17958E.description: Label and describe the functions of the basic parts of the male and female reproductive systems.

F09065D0DFE40131568E68A86D17958E.description: Label and describe the functions of the basic parts of the circulatory system including the heart, arteries, veins and capillaries.

F09025B0DFE40131568D68A86D17958E.description: Explain that human body systems are comprised of organs (e.g., the heart, the stomach, and the lungs) that perform specific functions within one or more systems.

F08FE300DFE40131568C68A86D17958E.description: Living systems demonstrate the complementary nature of structure and function.

F08F59D0DFE40131568A68A86D17958E.description: Cite three lines of evidence such as the fit of coastlines, the similarity of rock type and contiguousness of bedding areas, and similarity of fossilized remains that indicate that the continents were once a large land mass.

F08F0CC0DFE40131568968A86D17958E.description: Explain how sedimentary rocks are formed through the processes of weathering, erosion, and deposition.

F08EBCF0DFE40131568868A86D17958E.description: Describe the process by which eroded materials can form horizontal layers of sedimentary rock.

F08E6360DFE40131568768A86D17958E.description: Investigate how weathered materials are transported (i.e., mass movement and wind, water, and ice processes) in the process of erosion. Explain how erosion shapes rock particles.

F08E2100DFE40131568668A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe how factors such as abrasion, frost/ice wedging, temperature changes, and plant growth cause physical weathering of rocks. Infer the environment in which the sedimentary particles were formed based on the results of weathering.

F08DDF30DFE40131568568A86D17958E.description: Earth's components form systems. These systems continually interact at different rates of time, affecting the Earth locally and globally.

F08D9A20DFE40131568468A86D17958E.description: Examine sedimentary rock formations. Use relative dating and fossil evidence to correlate sedimentary rock sequences. Infer the succession of environmental events that occurred from one rock sequence to another (transgression or regression of the seas). Use the correlated sedimentary rock sequences to support Earth's geologic time scale.

F08D51B0DFE40131568368A86D17958E.description: Use appropriate instruments and tools to identify the sedimentary rocks: limestone, shale, and sandstone. Infer the environmental conditions in which these rocks formed.

F08CEF60DFE40131568268A86D17958E.description: Earth's systems can be broken down into individual components which have observable measurable properties.

F08BF800DFE40131567F68A86D17958E.description: Compare the differences in power usage in different electrical devices/appliances. Discuss which devices/appliances (i.e., washer, dryer, refrigerator, electric furnace) are manufactured to require less energy. Select one device/appliance, research different brands and their energy usage, determine which would be the better buy, and report on the findings.

F08BB460DFE40131567E68A86D17958E.description: People utilize a variety of resources to meet the basic and specific needs of life. Some of these resources cannot be replaced. Other resources can be replenished or exist in such vast quantities they are in no danger of becoming depleted. Often the energy stored in resources must be transformed into more useful forms and transported over great distances before it can be helpful to us.

F08B6EB0DFE40131567D68A86D17958E.description: Explain how these magnetic forces in electric motors are used to change the electrical energy into the energy of motion.

F08B21B0DFE40131567C68A86D17958E.description: Show how electrical energy carried by currents in wires can be used to create magnetic fields. Demonstrate how these fields exert magnetic forces on permanent magnets.

F08ADAD0DFE40131567B68A86D17958E.description: Energy readily transforms from one form to another, but these transformations are not always reversible. The details of these transformations depend upon the initial form of the energy and the properties of the materials involved. Energy may transfer into or out of a system and it may change forms, but the total energy cannot change.

F08A9B80DFE40131567A68A86D17958E.description: Design a device that relies on the directional and/or mechanical advantage of a simple machine to perform a task (e.g., lift a weight, move a heavy object). Identify the forces and motions involved, the source of the energy used to complete the task, and how the energy is used by the simple machine.

F08A5AE0DFE40131567968A86D17958E.description: Use the size of the force and the distance over which the force acts to compare how much energy is transferred into a simple machine to how much energy is transferred out of a simple machine.

F08A0DC0DFE40131567868A86D17958E.description: Explain that the transfer of energy from one object to another is caused by the exertion of a force.

F089BD60DFE40131567768A86D17958E.description: Conduct investigations using simple machines to demonstrate how forces transfer energy. Explain that simple machine may change the direction of an applied force (directional advantage) or the size of the force that is applied (mechanical advantage) but that the amount of energy transferred by the simple machine is equal to the amount of energy transferred to the simple machine.

F0896C40DFE40131567668A86D17958E.description: Explain that an object that feels the effects of balanced forces may be at rest or may be moving in a straight line with a speed that does not change.

F0890C90DFE40131567568A86D17958E.description: Conduct investigations and describe how a force can be directed to increase the speed of an object, decrease the speed of the object or change the direction in which the object moves.

F088CDA0DFE40131567468A86D17958E.description: Conduct investigations to describe how the relative directions of forces simultaneously acting on an object (reinforce or cancel each other) will determine how strongly the combination of these forces influences the motion of the object.

F0888D70DFE40131567368A86D17958E.description: Give examples of moving objects and identify the forces that act on these objects. Select examples where only one force acts on the object and examples where two or more forces act on the object. Explain that unbalanced forces acting on an object will change its speed, direction of motion, or both.

F0884D60DFE40131567268A86D17958E.description: Give examples of objects at rest, and identify the forces that act on an object while it remains at rest (gravity, supportive forces, friction, other pushing or pulling forces). Explain that if the object is not moving, it must have at least two forces acting on it that are balanced.

F0880CC0DFE40131567168A86D17958E.description: Explain that the earth will pull on all objects with a force called gravity that is directed inward toward the center of the Earth.

F087C900DFE40131567068A86D17958E.description: Describe how the speed of an object depends on the distance traveled and the travel time. Explain how the motion of an object can be described by its position, speed, and direction of motion.

F0876780DFE40131566F68A86D17958E.description: Graph and interpret distance versus time graphs for constant speed. Use the graphs to describe how the position of an object changes in a time interval.

F086EB90DFE40131566E68A86D17958E.description: Conduct investigations on a moving object and make measurements of time and distance traveled and determine the average speed of moving objects.

F086ACD0DFE40131566D68A86D17958E.description: Construct both series and parallel circuits to investigate and describe how multiple devices in series or parallel (bulbs, motors) perform (dim versus bright, fast versus slow). Describe how the way the devices are connected affects the functioning (i.e., dim versus bright) of the device, and relate this to how much electrical energy is received.

F0866E10DFE40131566C68A86D17958E.description: Relate that electrical energy carried by charges in a circuit is transferred to devices in the circuit and is usually changed into (transformed) different kinds of energy by these devices (e.g., light bulbs change electrical energy into light and heat energy, motors turn the electrical energy into energy of motion). Trace the flow of energy from electrical energy to other forms of energy, such as light. Express whether energy was transferred, transformed or both.

F0863000DFE40131566B68A86D17958E.description: Describe the role of electrical charge in circuits by using a model of electrical circuits.

F085ECE0DFE40131566A68A86D17958E.description: Changes take place because of the transfer of energy. Energy is transferred to matter through the action of forces. Different forces are responsible for the transfer of the different forms of energy.

F085A760DFE40131566968A86D17958E.description: Explain that electrical energy is a form of energy that is transferred through circuits to devices that are designed to make use of this form of energy (e.g., lamps, fans, computers, etc.).

F08559B0DFE40131566868A86D17958E.description: List, as basic forms of energy, light, heat, sound, electrical, and energy of motion.

F0851410DFE40131566768A86D17958E.description: Energy takes many forms. These forms can be grouped into types of energy that are associated with the motion of mass (kinetic energy) and types of energy associated with the position of mass and with energy fields (potential energy).

F0844960DFE40131566468A86D17958E.description: Use mathematics, reading, writing, and technology when conducting scientific inquiries.

F083E610DFE40131566368A86D17958E.description: Communicate scientific procedures, data, and explanations to enable the replication of results. Use computer technology to assist in communicating these results. Critical review is important in the analysis of these results.

F0837640DFE40131566268A86D17958E.description: Form explanations based on accurate and logical analysis of evidence. Revise the explanation using alternative descriptions, predictions, models and knowledge from other sources as well as results of further investigation.

F08327E0DFE40131566168A86D17958E.description: Accurately collect data through the selection and use of tools and techniques appropriate to the investigation. Construct tables, diagrams and graphs, showing relationships between two variables, to display and facilitate analysis of data. Compare and question results with and from other students.

F082DF50DFE40131566068A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct investigations with controlled variables to test hypotheses.

F0829150DFE40131565F68A86D17958E.description: Frame and refine questions that can be investigated scientifically, and generate testable hypotheses.

F0824330DFE40131565E68A86D17958E.description: Scientific inquiry involves asking scientifically-oriented questions, collecting evidence, forming explanations, connecting explanations to scientific knowledge and theory, and communicating and justifying the explanation.

F081E780DFE40131565D68A86D17958E.description: Nature and Application of Science and Technology

F301DCF0DFE401315B1068A86D17958E.description: Students will follow the actions of elected officials, and understand and employ the mechanisms for communicating with them while in office.

F301A270DFE401315B0F68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop and employ the civic skills necessary for effective, participatory citizenship [Participation].

F3016520DFE401315B0E68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand that American citizenship includes responsibilities such as voting, jury duty, obeying the law, service in the armed forces when required, and public service.

F3011FC0DFE401315B0D68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand that civil rights secure political freedom while property rights secure economic freedom and that both are essential protections for United States citizens.

F300CA20DFE401315B0C68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the responsibilities, rights, and privileges of United States citizens [Citizenship].

F3008CE0DFE401315B0B68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the principles and content of major American state papers such as the Declaration of Independence; United States Constitution (including the Bill of Rights); and the Federalist Papers.

F3005090DFE401315B0A68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand that the concept of majority rule does not mean that the rights of minorities may be disregarded and will examine and apply the protections accorded those minorities in the American political system.

F3001360DFE401315B0968A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the principles and ideals underlying the American political system [Politics].

F2FFD610DFE401315B0868A86D17958E.description: Students will analyze the different functions of federal, state, and local governments in the United States and examine the reasons for the different organizational structures each level of government employs.

F2FF9750DFE401315B0768A86D17958E.description: Students will understand that governments have the power to make and enforce laws and regulations, levy taxes, conduct foreign policy, and make war.

F2FF4B30DFE401315B0668A86D17958E.description: Students will examine the structure and purposes of governments with specific emphasis on constitutional democracy [Government].

F2E13710DFE401315AE368A86D17958E.description: Students will explain how conflict and cooperation among people contributes to the division of the Earth's surface into distinctive cultural regions and political territories.

F2E0F680DFE401315AE268A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the processes affecting the location of economic activities in different world regions.

F2E0A320DFE401315AE168A86D17958E.description: Students will develop an understanding of the character and use of regions and the connections between and among them [REGIONS].

F2E067B0DFE401315AE068A86D17958E.description: Students will identify and explain the major cultural patterns of human activity in the world's sub-regions.

F2E02A80DFE401315ADF68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop an understanding of the diversity of human culture and the unique nature of places [PLACES].

F2DFEC00DFE401315ADE68A86D17958E.description: Students will apply a knowledge of the major processes shaping natural environments to understand how different peoples have changed and been affected by, physical environments in the world's sub-regions.

F2DFA630DFE401315ADD68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop a knowledge of the ways humans modify and respond to the natural environment [ENVIRONMENT].

F2DF5BE0DFE401315ADC68A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate mental maps of the world and its sub-regions which include the relative location and characteristics of major physical features, political divisions, and human settlements.

F2DF09B0DFE401315ADB68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop a personal geographic framework, or "mental map," and understand the uses of maps and other geo-graphics [MAPS].

document.title: Delaware Theatre Content Standards and Grade Level Expectations

DF83F8B0DFE40131362568A86D17958E.description: Assess the social, cultural and economic impact of theater art on society

DF83AE80DFE40131362468A86D17958E.description: Analyze and explain the function of theater across cultures, times and places

DF836320DFE40131362368A86D17958E.description: Analyze dramatic works in the context of the culture, time and place in which they originated

DF831780DFE40131362268A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast different genres of theater (e.g., drama, comedy, musical theater, opera)

DF82CBD0DFE40131362168A86D17958E.description: Understanding theatre works in relation to cultures, times and places

DF8281F0DFE40131362068A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the artistic quality of a production based on established criteria

DF5FE9A0DFE40131361F68A86D17958E.description: Establish criteria for evaluating a presentation's effectiveness in communicating ideas and emotions

DF5FAB40DFE40131361E68A86D17958E.description: Explain how dramatic elements (plot, character, action, diction, music, spectacle, Aristotle's "Poetics", etc.) combine to make a whole

DF5F69B0DFE40131361D68A86D17958E.description: Assess how an audience's response can impact a theatrical presentation

DF5F2060DFE40131361C68A86D17958E.description: Relate the elements of a dramatic production and the impact they have on the viewer

DF5ED4F0DFE40131361B68A86D17958E.description: Identify and employ techniques for active listening and viewing of theatrical productions

DF5E8B00DFE40131361A68A86D17958E.description: Responding to, describing, analyzing, interpreting, and evaluating theatre works and performances

DF5E44A0DFE40131361968A86D17958E.description: Analyze the contributions of various art forms within a theatrical production (e.g., scenery, lighting, music, dance, costumes)

DF5DF8D0DFE40131361868A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast story lines presented through different artistic media (theater, dance, literature, music)

DF5DB620DFE40131361768A86D17958E.description: Incorporate elements of dance, music, and visual arts to express ideas and emotions in improvised and structured scenes

DF5D7140DFE40131361668A86D17958E.description: Observe different forms of communication and transfer them into usage in performance (verbal, nonverbal, ASL, written, iconic, etc.)

DF5D2700DFE40131361568A86D17958E.description: Observe examples of role playing in life and analyze how those roles could be used by theatre artists

DF5CA5E0DFE40131361368A86D17958E.description: Analyze and understand the importance of backstage needs and communicate a plan for managing backstage traffic, props and prop tables; dressing areas and costume changes; the use of wing space/backstage area and set units

DF5C6310DFE40131361268A86D17958E.description: Managing and producing informal and formal presentations

DF5C19D0DFE40131361168A86D17958E.description: Create a concept that conveys meaning for a scripted scene (be it linear, episodic, abstract) through the use of metaphor, mood or theme

DF5BB3A0DFE40131361068A86D17958E.description: Analyze the meaning of improvised or scripted scenes, scenarios and/or plays

DF5B6DB0DFE40131360F68A86D17958E.description: Directing by envisioning and realizing improvised or scripted scenes

DF5B2D50DFE40131360E68A86D17958E.description: Construct scenery and props appropriate to the setting of a theatrical production

DF5AEBF0DFE40131360D68A86D17958E.description: Apply design concepts (line, color, space, shape, texture) to design a set that communicates locale and mood for a theatrical production

DF5AAB10DFE40131360C68A86D17958E.description: Develop and implement costume and makeup designs for a structured theatrical production

DF5A6590DFE40131360B68A86D17958E.description: Designing and building environments for informal and formal presentations

DF5A1BF0DFE40131360A68A86D17958E.description: Apply various acting and performance methodologies to appropriate theatrical styles (DelSarte, Kabuki, Noh, Viewpoints, Theatre of the Oppressed, Theatre-in-Education, Restoration, etc.)

DF59D3F0DFE40131360968A86D17958E.description: Portray a believable character with effective performance techniques (use of voice, facial expressions and body movement) in both improvised and structured presentations

DF599850DFE40131360868A86D17958E.description: Identify character motivations through research and analysis and be able to articulate how they affect the character's actions

DF595C10DFE40131360768A86D17958E.description: Recall and recite assigned lines for a theater piece

DF591FE0DFE40131360668A86D17958E.description: Employ variations in movement, gesture and vocal expression (pitch, tempo, tone) to create characters

DF58DE30DFE40131360568A86D17958E.description: Acting in improvised and structured presentations

DF589F00DFE40131360468A86D17958E.description: Write an original oneact play with clearly developed characters, setting, conflict and resolution

DF585370DFE40131360368A86D17958E.description: Explore human issues and various outcomes in order to devise a performance piece that is linear in presentation form

DF580970DFE40131360268A86D17958E.description: Adapt a piece of literature into a theatrical piece

DF57C4E0DFE40131360168A86D17958E.description: Record the improvised movement and/or dialogue of a play through writing, taping or other means

DF578170DFE40131360068A86D17958E.description: Develop an improvisation utilizing characters and setting that creates tension and suspense, with a subsequent resolution

DF574160DFE4013135FF68A86D17958E.description: Identify the basic elements of a play (e.g., characters, setting, plot)

DF56FFE0DFE4013135FE68A86D17958E.description: Identify the foundation of playmaking in real life and fantasy

DF56B420DFE4013135FD68A86D17958E.description: Improvising and writing scenes, scenarios and plays

F3127860DFE401315B2568A86D17958E.description: Students will understand that the exchange of goods and services around the world creates economic interdependence between people in different places.

F3123D30DFE401315B2468A86D17958E.description: Students will examine the patterns and results of international trade [International trade].

F311FF60DFE401315B2368A86D17958E.description: Students will identify human wants and the various resources and strategies which have been used to satisfy them over time.

F311B390DFE401315B2268A86D17958E.description: Students will understand different types of economic systems and how they change [Economic systems].

F3117080DFE401315B2168A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how barter, money, and other media are employed to facilitate the exchange of resources, goods, and services.

F3112AB0DFE401315B2068A86D17958E.description: Students will examine the interaction of individuals, families, communities, businesses, and governments in a market economy [Macroeconomics].

F310E6A0DFE401315B1F68A86D17958E.description: Students will apply the concept that economic choices require the balancing of costs incurred with benefits received.

F3108AE0DFE401315B1E68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand that individuals and families with limited resources undertake a wide variety of activities to satisfy their wants.

F3102BB0DFE401315B1D68A86D17958E.description: Students will analyze the potential costs and benefits of personal economic choices in a market economy [Microeconomics].

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

comments: For example, how much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 1/3-cup servings are in 2 cups of raisins?
674E13E2810D4BA4BB5F255A6EC4C2B1.description: Solve real world problems involving division of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers and division of whole numbers by unit fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

54A69897DF8647E2814968819D7376EE.description: Interpret division of a whole number by a unit fraction, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for 4 ÷ (1/5), and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 because 20 × (1/5) = 4.

8A7B161E296C45379D2679A18D020F00.description: Interpret division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for (1/3) ÷ 4, and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 because (1/12) × 4 = 1/3.

Students able to multiply fractions in general can develop strategies to divide fractions in general, by reasoning about the relationship between multiplication and division. But division of a fraction by a fraction is not a requirement at this grade
1EEEDBAD86FF49B49123A14D6A7B6E12.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.

C17EDE3152A844DE9B641179CFA80ACC.description: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.

5476FAFC26A34699A9598E002C449526.description: Explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction greater than 1 results in a product greater than the given number (recognizing multiplication by whole numbers greater than 1 as a familiar case); explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction less than 1 results in a product smaller than the given number; and relating the principle of fraction equivalence a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) to the effect of multiplying a/b by 1.

0A49C17BE145418FB7FEEAE8E6EB87F1.description: Comparing the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.

386DD32BF07B43D59FA46981034FCC03.description: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. Multiply fractional side lengths to find areas of rectangles, and represent fraction products as rectangular areas.

comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)
78EB5DA3C3604A389026A837DC5DE22A.description: Interpret the product (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b.

8B6A31E57C074204BFBAF2CF85CF8B4B.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction.

comments: For example, interpret 3/4 as the result of dividing 3 by 4, noting that 3/4 multiplied by 4 equals 3, and that when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4 people each person has a share of size 3/4. If 9 people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds of rice should each person get? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
76FD016696F54815A6C2FC9CFCA20890.description: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.

4DC09D9D01C34166AA8BD21B8788CFF6.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.

DA47280D6EA94775819D291EA7CC7F02.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers.
comments: For example, recognize an incorrect result 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7, by observing that 3/7 < 1/2.

7A377E28724F497DA658B4B2D99EDE11.description: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators.
comments: For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.)

Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.

58F7AE7039224906962994782648F4A8.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.
